:::

The `mean` and `median` labels differ for `r sum(lisa$mean != lisa$median)` of the 330 townships and
for `r sum(lisa$p_ii_sim < 0.05 & lisa$mean != lisa$median)` of the `r sum(lisa$p_ii_sim < 0.05)`
significant townships. Of
the `r sum(lisa$armed > median(lisa$armed) & lisa$armed < mean(lisa$armed))` townships with a count
between the median and the
mean, `r n_mid_sig` `r if (n_mid_sig == 1) "township is" else "townships are"` significant.

### Clusters and spatial outliers of armed events

Local I, its p-value and the class are mapped separately, as in Hands-on Exercise 5 and Mack and
Kam (2018, Figures 10 to 12). Local I is positive where a township's count and its neighbours'
average are on the same side of the mean, and negative where the count and the neighbours' average
are on opposite sides. The size of local I shows the strength of this association in every
township, including the townships that are not significant. The p-value map shows the townships
with a pseudo p-value below 0.05 and below 0.01. A positive local I occurs in both High-High and
Low-Low townships, so the class map below gives each significant township a class from the position
of its count and of its spatial lag relative to the median (@sec-lisa-labels).

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Map

```{r}
#| label: lisa-maps
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 5.1
lisa_ii <- tm_shape(lisa) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "ii",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "pretty", n = 7, midpoint = 0,
                                              values = "-brewer.rd_bu"),
              col = "white", lwd = 0.15,
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "local I",
                                      position = tm_pos_out("right", "center"))) +
  tm_title("Local Moran's I", size = 1.2) + tm_layout(frame = FALSE) + map_extras

lisa_p <- tm_shape(lisa) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "p_ii_sim",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(breaks = c(0, 0.01, 0.05, 1),
                                              labels = c("below 0.01", "0.01 to 0.05",
                                                         "0.05 or above"),
                                              values = "-brewer.greys"),
              col = "white", lwd = 0.15,
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "p-value",
                                      position = tm_pos_out("right", "center"))) +
  tm_title("Pseudo p-value,\n999 permutations", size = 1.2) + tm_layout(frame = FALSE) + map_extras

tmap_arrange(lisa_ii, lisa_p, ncol = 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: lisa-summary
#| echo: false
hh <- lisa |> st_drop_geometry() |> filter(cluster == "High-High")
ll <- lisa |> st_drop_geometry() |> filter(cluster == "Low-Low")
hh_share <- sum(hh$armed) / sum(tsp$armed)
outl <- lisa |> st_drop_geometry() |> filter(cluster %in% c("High-Low", "Low-High"))
hh_idx <- which(lisa$cluster == "High-High")
hh$block <- n.comp.nb(subset(nb, seq_along(nb) %in% hh_idx))$comp.id
hh_blocks <- hh |>
  group_by(block) |>
  summarise(n = n(), states = as.character(knitr::combine_words(unique(ST), oxford_comma = FALSE)),
            towns = as.character(knitr::combine_words(TS, oxford_comma = FALSE)))
central <- hh_blocks |> slice_max(n, n = 1)
lag_armed <- st_lag(tsp$armed, nb, wt)
ox <- \(t) c(n = tsp$armed[tsp$TS == t], lag = round(lag_armed[tsp$TS == t]))
top_ns <- tibble(TS = tsp$TS, ST = tsp$ST, n = tsp$armed, lag = round(lag_armed),
                 p = lisa$p_ii_sim) |>
  filter(n >= quantile(tsp$armed, 0.9)) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
top_ns3 <- top_ns |> filter(p >= 0.05) |> slice_head(n = 3)
b8_named <- unique(c(hh$TS[hh$block != central$block], "Shwebo", "Monywa", "Pakokku", outl$TS,
                     top_ns3$TS, ll$TS[!str_detect(ll$ST, "Shan") &
                                         !ll$ST %in% c("Ayeyarwady", "Yangon", "Nay Pyi Taw")]))
ll_other <- with(ll, paste0(TS, " (", ST, ")")[!str_detect(ST, "Shan") &
                    !ST %in% c("Ayeyarwady", "Yangon", "Nay Pyi Taw")])
```

```{r}
named_cols <- \(cols) setNames(replace(cols, "Not significant", "grey70"),
                               sub("Not significant", named_ns, names(cols)))
named_group <- \(cl, cols) droplevels(factor(sub("Not significant", named_ns, cl),
                                             names(named_cols(cols))))
b8_sel <- lisa |>
  filter(cluster != "Not significant" | TS %in% b8_named) |>
  mutate(group = named_group(cluster, lisa_colours), lab = TS %in% b8_named)

             "Townships named in the text: local Moran's I classes") +
```

- **Bago (East):** `r hh_blocks$towns[str_detect(hh_blocks$states, "Bago")]` is the only High-High

## Local Geary's c {#sec-local-geary}

::: callout-note
## Local Geary's c: squared differences and cluster labels

Local Geary's c is the weighted sum of the squared differences between the standardised count of a
township and those of its neighbours (Anselin, 2019):

$$c_i = \sum_j w_{ij} (z_i - z_j)^2$$

$$\text{local } c = \sum \text{weight} \times (\text{standardised count} -
\text{neighbour's standardised count})^2$$

where $z_i$ and $z_j$ are the counts of townships $i$ and $j$, each minus the mean and divided by
the standard deviation. The formula on slide 27 of the Lesson 5 deck uses deviations from the mean;
`local_c_perm()` also divides them by the standard deviation, which changes the size of $c_i$ but
not its pseudo p-value. A small value means the township is similar to its neighbours; a large value
means it differs from them. "Since there is no cross-product involved, there is no direct relation
to linear similarity", so local Geary's c "may detect patterns that escape the Local Moran, and vice
versa" (Anselin, 2020b). Slide 27 of the Lesson 5 deck lists local Geary's c under other forms of
LISA.

Anselin (2019) first separates a small c (a township similar to its neighbours) from a large c (a
township different from its neighbours), then labels a small c by the township's count and its
neighbours' average. The labels in this report are those of Anselin (2019), with the dividing lines
at the median as for local Moran's I (@sec-lisa-labels):

| Label | Meaning |
|----------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| High-High | c is below its expected value, and the township's count and its neighbours' average are above their medians |
| Low-Low | c is below its expected value, and the township's count and its neighbours' average are at or below their medians |
| Other Positive | c is below its expected value, and the township's count and its neighbours' average are on different sides of their medians |
| Negative | c is above its expected value |
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Table

```{r}
#| label: local-geary
#| echo: false
set.seed(2610)
geary <- tsp |>
  mutate(local_c = local_c_perm(armed, nb, wt, nsim = 999), .before = 1) |>
  unnest(local_c) |>
  mutate(cluster = case_when(p_ci_sim >= 0.05 ~ "Not significant",
                             ci > e_ci ~ "Negative",
                             armed > median(armed) & lag_armed > median(lag_armed) ~ "High-High",
                             armed <= median(armed) & lag_armed <= median(lag_armed) ~ "Low-Low",
                             .default = "Other Positive"),
         cluster = factor(cluster, levels = c("High-High", "Low-Low", "Other Positive",
                                              "Negative", "Not significant")))
count(st_drop_geometry(geary), cluster) |> kable()
```

#### Code

```{r}
#| ref.label: "local-geary"
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
`local_c_perm()` returns local $c$ (`ci`), its permutation mean (`e_ci`) and its pseudo p-value. Its
`cluster` label is the same whether $c$ is small or large, so `case_when()` relabels the townships
after Anselin (2019): `ci` above `e_ci` is "Negative". Below it, a township is High-High or Low-Low
when its count and its spatial lag (`lag_armed`) are on the same side of their medians, and "Other
Positive" otherwise.

```{r}
#| label: geary-only
#| echo: false
geary_only <- tibble(TS = tsp$TS, ST = tsp$ST, moran = lisa$cluster, geary = geary$cluster) |>
  filter(geary == "High-High", moran != "High-High")
geary_tab <- tibble(TS = tsp$TS, ST = tsp$ST, n = tsp$armed, lag = round(st_lag(tsp$armed, nb, wt)),
                    geary = geary$cluster)
geary_neg <- filter(geary_tab, geary == "Negative")
geary_op <- filter(geary_tab, geary == "Other Positive")
op_n <- sum(geary_op$n > median(tsp$armed) & geary_op$lag <= median(lag_armed))
op_each <- if (op_n == nrow(geary_op)) "each of them" else paste(op_n, "of them")
cw <- \(x) knitr::combine_words(x, oxford_comma = FALSE)
lg_z <- \(x) (x - mean(x)) / sd(x)
near0 <- which(geary$cluster == "High-High" & lisa$cluster != "High-High" &
                 abs(lg_z(tsp$armed)) <= 0.4 & abs(lg_z(lag_armed)) <= 0.4)
mo_only <- which(lisa$cluster == "High-High" & geary$cluster != "High-High")
mo_gap <- abs(tsp$armed - lag_armed)[mo_only]
mo_ex <- mo_only[which.max(mo_gap)]
b8_geary_named <- unique(c(geary_only$TS[geary_only$ST == "Sagaing"], geary_neg$TS, geary_op$TS,
                            tsp$TS[near0], tsp$TS[mo_ex]))
```

Differences from local Moran's I:

- **High-High under local Geary only:** `r nrow(geary_only)` townships,
  in `r n_distinct(geary_only$ST)` states and regions, are High-High under local Geary's c and not

  the `r nrow(geary_only)` townships, the count and the neighbours' average are each within 0.4
  standard deviations of its own mean, so local Moran's I is at most `r sprintf("%.2f", max(lisa$ii[near0]))`: `r cw(tsp$TS[near0])`.
- **High-High under local Moran only:** `r length(mo_only)` townships are High-High under local
  Moran's I and in another class under local Geary's c. In `r sum(mo_gap > 100)` of them, the count and the
  neighbours' average differ by more than 100 events, for example `r tsp$TS[mo_ex]`
  (`r tsp$armed[mo_ex]` events, neighbours' average `r round(lag_armed[mo_ex])`).
- **Negative (c above its expected value):** the `r nrow(geary_neg)` townships
  are `r cw(paste0(geary_neg$TS, " (", geary_neg$n, " events, neighbours' average ", geary_neg$lag, ")"))`.
  Hlaingbwe is also a Low-High outlier under local Moran's I.
- **Other Positive:** this class has `r nrow(geary_op)` townships, `r sum(geary_op$ST == "Yangon")`
  of them in Yangon (`r cw(geary_op$TS[geary_op$ST == "Yangon"])`). The remaining township
  is `r cw(paste0(geary_op$TS[geary_op$ST != "Yangon"], " in ", geary_op$ST[geary_op$ST != "Yangon"]))`.
  The count is above its median and the neighbours' average is below its median in `r op_each`.

## Getis-Ord Gi and Gi\* {#sec-gi}

Getis and Ord (1992) define Gi\* as the weighted sum of the counts of a township and its neighbours,
divided by the sum of all counts (Lesson 5 slide 30):

$$G_i^* = \frac{\sum_j w_{ij} x_j}{\sum_j x_j}$$

$$\text{G}_i^* = \frac{\text{weighted sum of the counts of the township and its neighbours}}
{\text{sum of all counts}}$$

`local_gstar_perm()` returns Gi\* as a z-score: the weighted sum minus the same sum at the mean
count, divided by the standard deviation of that sum (Ord and Getis, 1995; Lesson 5 slide 31):

$$Z(G_i^*) = \frac{\sum_j w_{ij} x_j - \bar{x} \sum_j w_{ij}}
{S \sqrt{\left[ n \sum_j w_{ij}^2 - \left( \sum_j w_{ij} \right)^2 \right] / (n - 1)}}$$

$$Z(\text{G}_i^*) = \frac{\text{weighted sum of the counts} - \text{the same sum at the mean}}
{\text{standard deviation of that sum}}$$

where $x_j$ is the count of township $j$, $\bar{x}$ is the mean count, $w_{ij}$ is the
row-standardised weight, $n$ is the number of townships and $S$ is the standard deviation of the
counts. The sums over $j$ include the township itself. Gi is the same statistic without the
township's own count.

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Output

```{r}
#| label: gi
#| echo: false
nb_self <- include_self(nb)
wt_self <- st_weights(nb_self, style = "W")
spot_of <- \(z, p) case_when(p >= 0.05 ~ "Not significant", z > 0 ~ "Hot spot",
                             .default = "Cold spot")
set.seed(2610)
gistar <- tsp |>
  mutate(g = local_gstar_perm(armed, nb_self, wt_self, nsim = 999), .before = 1) |>
  unnest(g) |>
  mutate(spot = factor(spot_of(gi_star, p_sim), c("Hot spot", "Cold spot", "Not significant")))
set.seed(2610)
gi <- tsp |>
  mutate(g = local_g_perm(armed, nb, wt, nsim = 999), .before = 1) |>
  unnest(g) |>
  mutate(spot = factor(spot_of(gi, p_sim), c("Hot spot", "Cold spot", "Not significant")))
table(`Gi*` = gistar$spot, Gi = gi$spot)
```

```{r}
#| ref.label: "gi"
#| eval: false

```
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false

```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
`include_self()` adds each township to its own neighbour list, which turns Gi into Gi\*.
`local_gstar_perm()` and `local_g_perm()` return the z-score and the pseudo p-value, and `spot_of()`
labels hot and cold spots by the sign of the z-score where p < 0.05 (Getis and Ord, 1992). In-class
Exercise 5 maps the `cluster` column instead, which compares a township's own count with the mean,
and reads "Low" for `r sum(gi_low)` hot spots: `r cw(gistar$TS[gi_low])`.

In the invented example below, a township (orange) has three neighbours (blue). In `nb`, each
neighbour has the weight $1/3$ and the township has no entry, shown as 0. `include_self()` adds the
township as a fourth entry, and each of the four entries then has the weight $1/4$.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2.6
hex_at <- \(x, y, id) tibble(id = id, a = seq(30, 330, 60) * pi / 180) |>
  mutate(px = x + cos(a) * 0.98, py = y + sin(a) * 0.98)
is_cells <- tibble(cx = c(0, sqrt(3), -sqrt(3) / 2, -sqrt(3) / 2),
                   cy = c(0, 0, 1.5, -1.5), role = c("self", "nb", "nb", "nb")) |>
  crossing(panel = 1:2) |>
  mutate(cx = cx + (panel - 1) * 7, id = row_number(),
         w = case_when(panel == 2 ~ "1/4", role == "nb" ~ "1/3", .default = "0"))
is_hex <- pmap_dfr(list(is_cells$cx, is_cells$cy, is_cells$id), hex_at) |>
  left_join(select(is_cells, id, role), by = "id")
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = is_hex, aes(px, py, group = id, fill = role), colour = "grey40") +
  geom_text(data = is_cells, aes(cx, cy, label = w), size = 5, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = c(0.3, 7.3), y = 3.1, size = 4, fontface = "bold", lineheight = 0.9,
           label = c("nb: 3 neighbours,\nweight 1/3 each",
                     "nb_self: 4 entries,\nweight 1/4 each")) +
  annotate("segment", x = 2.9, xend = 4.9, y = 0, yend = 0, linewidth = 1.2,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm"))) +
  annotate("text", x = 3.9, y = 0.65, label = "include_self()", size = 3.4, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(self = "#fdd0a2", nb = "#c6dbef"), guide = "none") +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-1.9, 9.4), ylim = c(-2.6, 3.7)) +
  theme_void()
```

Gi and Gi\* give the same label to `r sum(gi$spot == gistar$spot)` of the 330 townships. In each of
the other `r sum(gi$spot != gistar$spot)` townships, the label is significant under one statistic
and not significant under the other. The p-values of these townships under Gi and Gi\* lie
between `r sprintf("%.3f", min(c(gi$p_sim, gistar$p_sim)[rep(gi$spot != gistar$spot, 2)]))`
and `r sprintf("%.3f", max(c(gi$p_sim, gistar$p_sim)[rep(gi$spot != gistar$spot, 2)]))`. No township
is a hot spot under one statistic and a cold spot under the other.

## Agreement between the four statistics {#sec-agreement}

Gi and Gi\* identify hot and cold spots. Local Moran's I and local Geary's c also identify spatial
outliers. Khan et al. (2017) use Gi\* for hot and cold spots and local Moran's I for spatial
outliers.

```{r}
#| label: agreement
#| code-fold: true
compare <- tibble(TS = tsp$TS, ST = tsp$ST, armed = tsp$armed,
                  moran = lisa$cluster, geary = geary$cluster, gistar = gistar$spot)
```

```{r}
#| label: robust-core
#| echo: false
core_hot <- compare |> filter(moran == "High-High", geary == "High-High", gistar == "Hot spot")
core_cold <- compare |> filter(moran == "Low-Low", geary == "Low-Low", gistar == "Cold spot")
```

Under both local Moran's I and local Geary's c, `r nrow(core_hot)` townships are High-High and are
Gi\* hot spots. Under the same two statistics, `r nrow(core_cold)` townships are Low-Low and are
Gi\* cold spots.

Each row of the chart below is one combination of the labels of local Moran's I, local Geary's c, Gi
and Gi\* for the same township, with the number of townships that have the combination.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.6
agree_combo <- compare |>
  mutate(gi = gi$spot) |>
  count(moran, geary, gi, gistar) |>
  filter(!(moran == "Not significant" & geary == "Not significant" & gistar == "Not significant" &
             gi == "Not significant")) |>
  arrange(desc(n)) |>
  mutate(row = row_number())
n_none <- sum(compare$moran == "Not significant" & compare$geary == "Not significant" &
                compare$gistar == "Not significant" & gi$spot == "Not significant")
agree_long <- agree_combo |>
  pivot_longer(c(moran, geary, gi, gistar), names_to = "statistic", values_to = "label") |>
  mutate(statistic = factor(statistic, c("moran", "geary", "gi", "gistar"),
                            c("Local Moran's I", "Local Geary's c", "Gi", "Gi*")),
         short = recode(as.character(label), "High-High" = "HH", "Low-Low" = "LL",
                        "High-Low" = "HL", "Low-High" = "LH", "Hot spot" = "hot",
                        "Cold spot" = "cold", "Negative" = "neg", "Other Positive" = "other +",
                        "Not significant" = ""))
agree_fill <- c("High-High" = "#CB181D", "Low-Low" = "#2171B5", "High-Low" = "#FB9A99",
                "Low-High" = "#A6CEE3", "Hot spot" = "#CB181D", "Cold spot" = "#2171B5",
                "Negative" = "#FB9A99", "Other Positive" = "#fdd0a2", "Not significant" = "grey88")
ggplot(agree_long, aes(as.integer(statistic), -row)) +
  geom_tile(aes(fill = label), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.8, width = 0.95, height = 0.9) +
  geom_text(aes(label = short, colour = label %in% c("High-High", "Low-Low", "Hot spot",
                                                      "Cold spot")), size = 3) +
  geom_text(data = agree_combo, aes(x = 4.75, y = -row, label = n), hjust = 0, size = 3.2) +
  annotate("text", x = c(1:4, 4.75), y = 0.1, hjust = c(rep(0.5, 4), 0), size = 3.2,
           fontface = "bold", label = c(levels(agree_long$statistic), "townships")) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.55, y = -nrow(agree_combo) - 1, hjust = 0, size = 3.2,
           label = paste("Not significant under all four statistics:", n_none, "townships")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = agree_fill, guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "white", `FALSE` = "grey20"), guide = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.5, 5.4), ylim = c(-nrow(agree_combo) - 1.3, 0.6)) +
  theme_void()
```

## Weights: Queen contiguity versus k-nearest neighbours {#sec-weights-check}

Mack and Kam (2018) compute Moran's I and Geary's C under several weight matrices, including
k-nearest neighbours with $k$ from 8 to 28, as a calibration. Mack and Kam (2018, p. 7) find that
"the increase in the number of neighbors have the effect of smoothening out the Moran's I scores",
with the highest Moran's I at $k = 8$ and the lowest at $k = 28$. Global Moran's I is computed here
under Queen contiguity and under k-nearest neighbours with $k = 6$ and $k = 8$.

```{r}
#| label: k-smooth
#| echo: false
ks <- map_dfr(c(6, 8, 16, 28), \(k) {
  n <- st_knn(pos, k = k)
  lw <- nb2listw(n, style = "W")
  far <- map2_dbl(n, seq_along(n), \(j, i) max(as.numeric(st_distance(pos[i], pos[j]))))
  tibble(k = k, `median distance to the farthest neighbour (km)` = round(median(far) / 1000),
         `spread of the spatial lags (SD)` = round(sd(lag.listw(lw, tsp$armed))),
         `Moran's I` = round(moran(tsp$armed, lw, length(n), Szero(lw))$I, 3))
})
```

::: callout-note
## Spatial lags under a high $k$: the smoothing effect

Each township's spatial lag is the average count of its $k$ nearest townships. As $k$ grows, the
average covers more distant townships and more townships with high and with low counts, so the lags are closer
to the national mean and differ less from one township to the next. Moran's I compares each township's
count with its lag, so it falls:

```{r}
#| echo: false
kable(ks)
```

For comparison, the counts themselves have a standard deviation of `r round(sd(tsp$armed))` events.
$k = 28$ is the largest value that Mack and Kam (2018) tested.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Table

```{r}
#| label: weights-check
#| echo: false
schemes <- list(`Queen, islands linked` = nb,
                `k-nearest, k = 6` = st_knn(pos, k = 6),
                `k-nearest, k = 8` = st_knn(pos, k = 8))
set.seed(2610)
wcheck <- imap_dfr(schemes, \(n, name) {
  g <- global_moran_perm(tsp$armed, n, st_weights(n, style = "W"), nsim = 999)
  tibble(weights = name, `mean neighbours` = mean(card(n)), `Moran's I` = g$statistic,
         p = fmt_p(g$p.value))
})
kable(wcheck, digits = 3)
wI <- round(wcheck[["Moran's I"]], 3)
```

#### Code

```{r}
#| ref.label: "weights-check"
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
```
:::

Moran's I is highest under Queen contiguity and falls from $k = 6$ to $k = 8$, in line with the
finding of Mack and Kam (2018) for Africa. Moran's I is significant at p ≤ 0.001 under each of the
three weights.

The table below lists the share of townships with the same local Moran's I class under each pair of
weights (Queen contiguity, $k = 6$ and $k = 8$):

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Table

```{r}
#| label: agreement-weights
#| echo: false
set.seed(2610)
lisa_under <- imap(schemes, \(n, name) {
  lm <- local_moran(tsp$armed, n, st_weights(n, style = "W"), nsim = 999)
  if_else(lm$p_ii_sim < 0.05, as.character(lm$median), "Not significant")
})
agree_w <- tibble(comparison = c("Queen, islands linked, against k = 6",
                      "Queen, islands linked, against k = 8",
                      "k = 6 against k = 8"),
       `same LISA class` = c(mean(lisa_under[[1]] == lisa_under[[2]]),
                             mean(lisa_under[[1]] == lisa_under[[3]]),
                             mean(lisa_under[[2]] == lisa_under[[3]])))
kable(agree_w, digits = 2)
changed_pct <- round(100 * (1 - agree_w[["same LISA class"]]))
```

#### Code

```{r}
#| ref.label: "agreement-weights"
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
```

Under $k = 6$, the local Moran class differs from the Queen contiguity class for `r changed_pct[1]`%
of the townships. Under $k = 8$, the class differs for `r changed_pct[2]`%.

## Multiple comparisons: false discovery rate correction {#sec-fdr}

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Table

```{r}
#| label: fdr
#| echo: false
tibble(statistic = c("local Moran's I", "local Geary's c", "Gi*"),
       p = list(lisa$p_ii_sim, geary$p_ci_sim, gistar$p_sim)) |>
  mutate(`p < 0.05` = map_int(p, \(x) sum(x < 0.05)),
         `FDR q < 0.05` = map_int(p, \(x) sum(p.adjust(x, method = "BH") < 0.05))) |>
  select(-p) |>
  kable()
```

#### Code

```{r}
#| ref.label: "fdr"
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
`p.adjust(method = "BH")` applies the Benjamini-Hochberg correction, which keeps the expected share
of false discoveries among the significant townships at 5% or less.
:::
:::

::: callout-note
## Benjamini-Hochberg correction: a worked example

Example: four townships have the p-values 0.01, 0.02, 0.04 and 0.30, so $m = 4$ (the report has
$m = 330$). Three are below 0.05. The correction sorts the p-values and multiplies the p-value of
rank $i$ by $m/i$:

| Township | p | Rank $i$ | $p \times 4/i$ | Below 0.05 before | Below 0.05 after |
|----------|------|----------|-----------------------------|-------------------|------------------|
| A | 0.01 | 1 | $0.01 \times 4/1 = 0.04$ | yes | yes |
| B | 0.02 | 2 | $0.02 \times 4/2 = 0.04$ | yes | yes |
| C | 0.04 | 3 | $0.04 \times 4/3 = 0.053$ | yes | **no** |
| D | 0.30 | 4 | $0.30 \times 4/4 = 0.30$ | no | no |

Township C changes: its adjusted p-value of 0.053 is above 0.05, so two of the three significant
townships remain significant. When an adjusted value is larger than the value of the next rank,
`p.adjust()` lowers it to that value; no value needs lowering in this example.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fdr-counts
#| echo: false
p_bh <- p.adjust(lisa$p_ii_sim, "BH")
fdr_hh <- sum(lisa$cluster == "High-High" & p_bh < 0.05)
fdr_ll <- sum(lisa$cluster == "Low-Low" & p_bh < 0.05)
```

After the Benjamini-Hochberg correction, `r fdr_hh + fdr_ll` of the `r nrow(hh) + nrow(ll)`
High-High and Low-Low townships of local Moran's I remain significant:

- **High-High:** `r fdr_hh` of the `r nrow(hh)` High-High townships remain significant.
- **Low-Low:** `r fdr_ll` of the `r nrow(ll)` Low-Low townships remain significant.

A township with p < 0.05 and an adjusted p-value of 0.05 or more has weaker evidence of belonging to
its cluster.

# Emerging hot spot analysis {#sec-ehsa}

Local measures describe the whole period at once. A whole-period map gives the same label to a
township that fell from a hot spot in 2021 to few events by 2025 and to one that rose over the same
period. Emerging hot spot analysis assigns different classes to a rising and a falling pattern. It
computes Gi\* for every township in every quarter, then tests each township's series of Gi\* values
for a trend (Lesson 5 slides 40 to 46).

## The space-time cube {#sec-cube}

::: callout-note
## Space-time cube: townships by quarters

A space-time cube holds one value for every location in every time period. Here the locations are
the 330 townships and the periods are the 19 quarters, so the cube has 330 × 19 = 6,270 cells. Each
cell holds the number of armed events in one township in one quarter. A township with no event in a
quarter has the value 0, which is a count of no events. `is_spacetime_cube()` also requires every
township and quarter pair to be present.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 3.3
show_ts <- c("Monywa", "Myaing", "Kyaukkyi", "Hpakant", "Maungdaw", "Laukkaing",
             "Hlaingtharya (East)", "Mongla")
q_counts |>
  left_join(st_drop_geometry(tsp)[, c("TS_PCODE", "TS")], by = "TS_PCODE") |>
  filter(TS %in% show_ts) |>
  mutate(TS = factor(TS, rev(show_ts))) |>
  ggplot(aes(quarter, TS, fill = n)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), size = 2.8, colour = "grey15") +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Reds", direction = 1, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_date(date_labels = "%Y", date_breaks = "1 year") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Eight of the 330 rows of the cube: armed events per quarter") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
```

Each row is one township's time series, and each column is one quarter's map. Emerging hot spot
analysis computes Gi\* in each quarter (the columns), then tests each township's Gi\* values for a
trend (the rows).
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Output

```{r}
#| label: cube
#| echo: false
cube_data <- q_counts |>
  rename(armed = n) |>
  mutate(t = as.integer(factor(quarter))) |>
  arrange(TS_PCODE, t)

geo <- tsp |> select(TS_PCODE, TS, ST)
cube <- spacetime(cube_data, geo, .loc_col = "TS_PCODE", .time_col = "t")
is_spacetime_cube(cube)
```

```{r}
#| ref.label: "cube"
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
```

## Gi\* by quarter: hot and cold spots {#sec-gi-quarter}

The neighbours and weights are stored with the cube geometry and used in every quarter: Queen
contiguity with linked islands, each township as its own neighbour, and row-standardised
weights (@sec-gistar).

```{r}
#| label: gi-quarter
#| code-fold: true
cube <- cube |>
  activate("geometry") |>
  mutate(nb = nb_self, wt = wt_self) |>
  set_nbs("nb") |>
  set_wts("wt") |>
  activate("data")

set.seed(2610)
gi_q <- cube |>
  group_by(t) |>
  mutate(gi_star = local_gstar_perm(armed, nb, wt, nsim = 99)) |>
  unnest(gi_star) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(quarter = quarters[t],
         spot = factor(spot_of(gi_star, p_sim), c("Hot spot", "Cold spot", "Not significant")))
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
`activate("geometry")`, `set_nbs()` and `set_wts()` attach the Gi\* neighbours and weights to every
quarter, and `group_by(t)` computes Gi\* within each quarter with 99 permutations, as in In-class
Exercise 6.

The data layer of `cube` after `set_nbs()` and `set_wts()`, with the new columns shaded. The

## Mann-Kendall test: trends in the Gi\* series {#sec-mk}

::: callout-note
## Mann-Kendall test: the score $S$ and Kendall's $\tau$

The test compares every quarter with every later quarter in one township's series. A later value
above the earlier one scores +1, a later value below scores -1, and a tie scores 0 (Helsel et al.,
2020, p. 217). The sum of these scores is $S$. Kendall's $\tau$ is $S$ divided by the number of
pairs of quarters:

$$S = \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} \sum_{j=k+1}^{n} \operatorname{sgn}(x_j - x_k), \quad
\tau = \frac{S}{n(n - 1)/2}$$

$$S = \text{pairs with a rise} - \text{pairs with a fall}, \quad
\tau = \frac{S}{\text{pairs of quarters}}$$

where $x_k$ and $x_j$ are the values in quarters $k$ and $j$, and $n$ is the number of quarters. The
formula of $\tau$ is for a series without ties; `MannKendall()` adjusts $\tau$ for tied values.
$\tau$ ranges from $-1$ for a series that falls at every step to $+1$ for a series that rises at
every step. The null hypothesis is no monotonic trend. Only the direction of each change enters the
sum, so $\tau$ is unchanged if every count is replaced by its rank.

```{r}
#| echo: false
toy <- c(1.2, 0.8, 1.9, 2.4, 2.1, 3.0)
pairs <- combn(seq_along(toy), 2)
s <- sum(sign(toy[pairs[2, ]] - toy[pairs[1, ]]))
mk_toy <- Kendall::MannKendall(toy)
tibble(quarter = as.character(1:6), `Gi*` = sprintf("%.1f", toy)) |>
  t() |> as.data.frame() |> kable(col.names = NULL)
```

Of the 15 pairs, `r sum(sign(toy[pairs[2, ]] - toy[pairs[1, ]]) > 0)` are rises
and `r sum(sign(toy[pairs[2, ]] - toy[pairs[1, ]]) < 0)` are falls, so $S$ = `r s` and $\tau$
= `r round(mk_toy$tau, 2)`, with a Mann-Kendall p-value of `r round(mk_toy$sl, 3)`.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Table

```{r}
#| label: mk-all
#| echo: false
mk <- gi_q |>
  group_by(TS_PCODE) |>
  summarise(mk = list(unclass(Kendall::MannKendall(gi_star)))) |>
  unnest_wider(mk) |>
  left_join(st_drop_geometry(geo), by = "TS_PCODE")

mk |>
  mutate(trend = case_when(sl >= 0.05 ~ "no significant trend",
                           tau > 0 ~ "Gi* rising", .default = "Gi* falling")) |>
  count(trend) |>
  kable()
```

two quarters. The Mann-Kendall test compares every pair of the 19 quarters, so one unusually high or
low quarter changes at most 18 of the 171 scores that make up $S$.

## Emerging hot spot classes {#sec-ehsa-classes}

::: callout-note
## Emerging hot spot classes: definitions

The definitions are those of the Lesson 5 slides (slides 44 and 45), which are based on ESRI's
emerging hot spot tool. Boschan and Roman (2024, Table 1) and Kim and Lee (2023, Table 1) use the
same set of classes. Each cold spot class has the same definition as the hot spot class of the same
name, with cold spots in place of hot spots.

| Class | Definition |
|---------------------|------------------------------------------------------------|
| New | hot in the final quarter and in no earlier quarter |
| Consecutive | hot in an unbroken run of at least two quarters at the end, in no quarter before the run, and in under 90% of all quarters |
| Intensifying | hot in at least 90% of quarters including the last, with a significant upward Mann-Kendall trend in Gi\* |
| Persistent | hot in at least 90% of quarters, with no significant Mann-Kendall trend in Gi\* |
| Diminishing | hot in at least 90% of quarters including the last, with a significant downward Mann-Kendall trend in Gi\* |
| Sporadic | hot in the final quarter and in some earlier quarters, in under 90% of quarters, and never a cold spot |
| Oscillating | hot in the final quarter and in under 90% of quarters, and a cold spot in at least one earlier quarter |
| Historical | hot in at least 90% of quarters, and not hot in the final quarter |
| No pattern detected | none of the above |

With 19 quarters, 90% means at least 18 quarters. The `sfdep` implementation differs from the slides
in two classes. In `sfdep`, a township is Sporadic when it has at least one significant hot quarter,
hot quarters are under 90% of the quarters, and it has no significant cold quarter, whether or not
the final quarter is hot. In the Persistent class, a Mann-Kendall p-value above 0.01 means no
significant trend.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Output

```{r}
#| label: ehsa
#| echo: false
set.seed(2610)
ehsa <- emerging_hotspot_analysis(cube, .var = "armed", k = 1, nsim = 99,
                                  nb_col = "nb", wt_col = "wt", include_gi = TRUE)
identical(ehsa$location, geo$TS_PCODE)

ehsa_gi <- attr(ehsa, "gi_star") |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(TS_PCODE = rep(geo$TS_PCODE, times = 19), t = rep(1:19, each = 330),
         quarter = quarters[t])

ehsa <- ehsa |>
  left_join(st_drop_geometry(geo), by = c(location = "TS_PCODE")) |>
  mutate(class = if_else(p_value < 0.05, classification, "not significant"))
count(ehsa, class, sort = TRUE) |> kable()
```

#### Code

```{r}
#| ref.label: "ehsa"
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
`emerging_hotspot_analysis()` computes Gi\* for every township and quarter, tests each series with
Mann-Kendall and assigns a class. `nb_col` and `wt_col` pass the cube's own neighbours: without them
the function builds plain Queen contiguity, which leaves the islands without neighbours. `k = 1`
adds the previous quarter to each neighbourhood, and a quarter counts as hot or cold at p ≤ 0.01.
`include_gi = TRUE` returns the Gi\* values used, and the final `mutate()` keeps the classes with a
Mann-Kendall p-value below 0.05, as the exercise requires.
:::
:::

::: callout-note
## Space-time neighbourhood: the previous quarter with `k = 1`

In the invented example below, a grid of 12 townships is drawn for three consecutive quarters, and
township C is in the middle row. With Queen contiguity and C counted as its own neighbour, the
neighbourhood of C is the nine shaded townships of the left three columns. With `k = 1`, Gi\* of C
in quarter $t$ uses the counts of those nine townships in quarter $t$ and in quarter $t - 1$. The
same weights from `wt` are applied to the cells of each quarter. The fourth column and quarter $t -
2$ are outside the neighbourhood. In quarter 1 there is no previous quarter, so Gi\* of quarter 1
uses the nine townships of quarter 1 only.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 2
ek_grid <- expand_grid(panel = 1:3, row = 1:3, col = 1:4) |>
  mutate(x = col + (panel - 1) * 5, y = 4 - row,
         used = col %in% 1:3 & panel %in% 2:3,
         centre = row == 2 & col == 2,
         count = c(0, 1, 0, 2, 3, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0, 2, 1,
                   1, 2, 0, 3, 4, 1, 2, 1, 0, 0, 3, 2,
                   2, 3, 1, 4, 6, 2, 3, 2, 1, 0, 2, 1),
         label = if_else(centre, paste0("C\n", count), as.character(count)))
ek_head <- tibble(x = c(2.5, 7.5, 12.5), y = 4.1,
                  label = c("Quarter t \u2212 2:\nnot used", "Quarter t \u2212 1:\nused (k = 1)",
                            "Quarter t:\nused"))
ggplot(ek_grid) +
  geom_tile(aes(x, y, fill = used), colour = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_tile(data = filter(ek_grid, centre, panel == 3), aes(x, y), fill = NA,
            colour = "grey15", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_text(aes(x, y, label = label), size = 3.6, lineheight = 0.85) +
  geom_text(data = ek_head, aes(x, y, label = label), size = 3.6, fontface = "bold",
            lineheight = 0.9) +
  annotate("text", x = 7.5, y = -0.05, size = 3.6, label = paste(
    "emerging_hotspot_analysis(k = 1): Gi* of C in quarter t uses the 18 shaded cells")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#ffc107", `FALSE` = "grey90"), guide = "none") +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0.4, 14.6), ylim = c(-0.3, 4.7)) +
  theme_void()
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: ehsa-lists
#| echo: false
in_class <- \(cl) ehsa |> filter(class == cl) |> mutate(x = paste0(TS, " (", ST, ")")) |> pull(x) |>
  knitr::combine_words(oxford_comma = FALSE)
n_class <- \(cl) sum(ehsa$class == cl)
n_in <- \(cl, st) sum(ehsa$class == cl & ehsa$ST == st)
all_rising <- \(cl) all(ehsa$tau[ehsa$class == cl] > 0)
all_of <- \(a, b) if (a == b) paste("all", a) else paste(a, "of the", b)
n_dir <- \(cl, up, st = unique(ehsa$ST)) sum(ehsa$class == cl & (ehsa$tau > 0) == up &
                                                ehsa$ST %in% st)
se3 <- c("Kayin", "Tanintharyi", "Mon")
spor_sag <- all_of(n_dir("sporadic hotspot", FALSE, "Sagaing"), n_in("sporadic hotspot", "Sagaing"))
spor_shn <- all_of(n_dir("sporadic hotspot", FALSE, "Shan (North)"),
                   n_in("sporadic hotspot", "Shan (North)"))
spor_se <- all_of(n_dir("sporadic hotspot", TRUE, se3),
                  sum(ehsa$class == "sporadic hotspot" & ehsa$ST %in% se3))
spor_c <- sort(table(ehsa$ST[ehsa$class == "sporadic coldspot"]), decreasing = TRUE)
spor_top <- head(spor_c, 6)
spor_list <- knitr::combine_words(paste(names(spor_top), spor_top), oxford_comma = FALSE)
cc_neg <- all(ehsa$tau[ehsa$class == "consecutive coldspot"] < 0)
cc_list <- in_class("consecutive coldspot")
cc_sentence <- if (cc_neg) "Every one of these townships has a negative Mann-Kendall tau." else ""
np <- ehsa |>
  filter(class == "no pattern detected") |>
  left_join(st_drop_geometry(tsp)[, c("TS_PCODE", "DT")], by = c(location = "TS_PCODE"))
np_n <- \(cond) sum(cond)
np_ygn <- np_n(np$ST == "Yangon"); np_ygn_down <- np_n(np$ST == "Yangon" & np$tau < 0)
np_mdy <- np_n(np$DT == "Mandalay"); np_mdy_down <- np_n(np$DT == "Mandalay" & np$tau < 0)
np_rkh <- np_n(np$ST == "Rakhine"); np_rkh_up <- np_n(np$ST == "Rakhine" & np$tau > 0)
np_kyh <- np_n(np$ST == "Kayah"); np_kyh_down <- np_n(np$ST == "Kayah" & np$tau < 0)
np_rest <- nrow(np) - np_ygn - np_mdy - np_rkh - np_kyh
np_rest_st <- n_distinct(np$ST[!(np$ST %in% c("Yangon", "Rakhine", "Kayah") | np$DT == "Mandalay")])
```

**Hot spot classes**

- **Consecutive hot spots (`r n_class("consecutive hotspot")`):** these townships have an unbroken
  run of significant hot quarters at the end of the
  period`r if (all_rising("consecutive hotspot")) ", and each has a positive Mann-Kendall tau" else ""`.
- **Oscillating hot spots (`r n_class("oscilating hotspot")`):** every township in this class was a
  significant cold spot in at least one earlier quarter and is a hot spot in the last quarter.
- **Mandalay
  Region:** `r n_in("consecutive hotspot", "Mandalay") + n_in("oscilating hotspot", "Mandalay")` of
  the `r n_class("consecutive hotspot") + n_class("oscilating hotspot")` townships in the
  consecutive and oscillating hot spot classes are in Mandalay Region. Armed events in Mandalay
  Region rose from `r yc("Mandalay", 2021)` in 2021 to `r yc("Mandalay", 2024)` in
  2024 (@sec-geovis).
- **Sporadic hot spots (`r n_class("sporadic hotspot")`):** each sporadic hot spot was hot in some
  quarters and cold in none. Gi\* has a significant downward Mann-Kendall trend
  in `r n_dir("sporadic hotspot", FALSE)` of them, including `r spor_sag` in Sagaing
  and `r spor_shn` in northern Shan. Gi\* has a significant upward trend in the
  other `r n_dir("sporadic hotspot", TRUE)`, including `r spor_se` in Kayin, Tanintharyi and Mon.

**Cold spot classes**

- **Consecutive cold spots
  (`r n_class("consecutive coldspot")`):** `r all_of(sum(ehsa$class == "consecutive coldspot" & ehsa$ST == "Yangon"), n_class("consecutive coldspot"))`
  are in Yangon Region (table above). `r cc_sentence`
- **Sporadic cold spots (`r n_class("sporadic coldspot")`):** `r spor_list`, and the
  other `r n_class("sporadic coldspot") - sum(spor_top)` are
  in `r length(spor_c) - length(spor_top)` other states and regions. The cold spots in Yangon Region
  match the fall in Yangon's armed events after 2022 (@sec-geovis).

**No pattern detected (`r n_class("no pattern detected")`).** These townships have a significant
Mann-Kendall trend in Gi\*, and their hot and cold quarters fit no other class.

| Where | Townships | Direction of Gi\* |
|-------------------------------------------|---------|------------------------------|
| Yangon Region | `r np_ygn` | falls in `r all_of(np_ygn_down, np_ygn)` |
| Mandalay District (Mandalay city and Amarapura) | `r np_mdy` | falls in `r all_of(np_mdy_down, np_mdy)` |
| Kayah State | `r np_kyh` | falls in `r all_of(np_kyh_down, np_kyh)` |
| Rakhine coast, Sittwe to Toungup | `r np_rkh` | rises in `r all_of(np_rkh_up, np_rkh)` |
| `r np_rest_st` other states and regions | `r np_rest` | n/a |

### Mann-Kendall p < 0.05 filter: townships removed {#sec-ehsa-filter}

The exercise requires maps of the townships significant at p < 0.05. The p-value that
`emerging_hotspot_analysis()` returns is the Mann-Kendall p-value of the township's Gi\* series.
Filtering on this p-value keeps only townships whose Gi\* has a significant monotonic trend.
Boschan and Roman (2024, Table 4) report every emerging hot spot class without a filter on the
Mann-Kendall p-value.

```{r}
#| label: filter-effect
#| echo: false
ft <- table(ehsa$classification, ehsa$p_value < 0.05)
kept <- \(cl) ft[cl, "TRUE"]; all_n <- \(cl) sum(ft[cl, ])
ph_note <- if (!"persistent hotspot" %in% rownames(ft)) {
  "No township is a persistent hot spot before the filter."
} else ""
```

In `sfdep`, a township is Persistent only if its Mann-Kendall p-value is above 0.01, so a persistent
township passes the filter only with a p-value between 0.01 and 0.05. The filter
keeps `r kept("persistent coldspot")` of the `r all_n("persistent coldspot")` persistent cold spots.
The sporadic classes depend on the quarters being hot or cold, so the filter keeps a sporadic
township only when its Gi\* also has a significant trend. The filter
keeps `r kept("sporadic coldspot")` of the `r all_n("sporadic coldspot")` sporadic cold spots
and `r kept("sporadic hotspot")` of the `r all_n("sporadic hotspot")` sporadic hot
spots. `r ph_note`

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Table

```{r}
#| label: ehsa-filter
#| echo: false
ehsa |>
  mutate(kept = if_else(p_value < 0.05, "Mann-Kendall p < 0.05", "p >= 0.05, removed")) |>
  count(classification, kept) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = kept, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  kable()

ehsa |>
  left_join(tibble(location = tsp$TS_PCODE, lisa = as.character(lisa$cluster)), by = "location") |>
  filter(lisa == "High-High") |>
  count(kept = p_value < 0.05, classification) |>
  kable()
```

```{r}
#| label: removed-hh
#| echo: false
pc <- ehsa$ST[ehsa$classification == "persistent coldspot"]
rm_hh <- ehsa$location[ehsa$p_value >= 0.05 &
                         ehsa$location %in% tsp$TS_PCODE[lisa$cluster == "High-High"]]
rise_fall <- ehsa_gi |>
  filter(TS_PCODE %in% rm_hh) |>
  group_by(TS_PCODE) |>
  summarise(rf = mean(gi_star[t %in% 6:13]) > max(mean(gi_star[t <= 4]), mean(gi_star[t >= 16])))
```

All `r length(pc)` persistent cold spots are removed: `r sum(str_detect(pc, "Shan"))` townships in
Shan State and `r sum(pc == "Ayeyarwady")` townships in the Ayeyarwady delta, each a cold spot in at
least 18 of the 19 quarters. The only new hot spot, Hpakant in Kachin, is removed as well
(p `r round(ehsa$p_value[ehsa$TS == "Hpakant"], 2)`). The filter also removes `r length(rm_hh)` of
the `r nrow(hh)` High-High townships of local Moran's I, including Monywa, Shwebo and Pakokku.
In `r all_of(sum(rise_fall$rf), length(rm_hh))` of these townships, the mean Gi\* of quarters 6 to
13 is above the mean of the first four quarters and the mean of the last four, so Gi\* rose and then
fell. The Mann-Kendall test detects only a monotonic trend, so a rise followed by a fall gives a
non-significant result. The filtered map shows where Gi\* has a significant monotonic trend. The
local measures in @sec-lmsa show where conflict has been concentrated.

## Serial correlation in the Gi\* series {#sec-serial}

According to slide 41 of the Lesson 5 deck, the Mann-Kendall test is non-parametric, and the data
"should have no serial correlation." Putrenko et al. (2018, p. 78) give the null hypothesis of the
test as "the data come from a population with independent realizations and are identically
distributed." Positive serial correlation inflates the variance of the Mann-Kendall statistic, so
the uncorrected test gives too many significant trends (Hamed and Rao, 1998). Hamed and Rao (1998)
correct the variance with the autocorrelations of the ranks of the detrended series.

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Table

```{r}
#| label: serial
#| echo: false
serial <- ehsa_gi |>
  arrange(TS_PCODE, t) |>
  group_by(TS_PCODE) |>
  summarise(r1 = acf(gi_star, lag.max = 1, plot = FALSE)$acf[2],
            p_hr = suppressWarnings(mmkh(gi_star))[["new P-value"]], .groups = "drop") |>
  left_join(select(ehsa, location, TS, p_value, class), by = c(TS_PCODE = "location"))
r1_crit <- qnorm(0.975) / sqrt(n_distinct(ehsa_gi$t))

serial |>
  filter(p_value < 0.05) |>
  mutate(corrected = case_when(is.na(p_hr) ~ "not computed",
                               p_hr < 0.05 ~ "p < 0.05", .default = "p ≥ 0.05")) |>
  count(class, corrected) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = corrected, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  kable()

sig_n <- sum(serial$p_value < 0.05)
kept_n <- sum(serial$p_value < 0.05 & serial$p_hr < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
lost <- serial |> filter(p_value < 0.05, p_hr >= 0.05)
na_ts <- serial$TS[is.na(serial$p_hr)]
```

#### Code

```{r}
#| ref.label: "serial"
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
`acf()` gives the lag-1 autocorrelation of each Gi\* series, and `mmkh()` reruns the Mann-Kendall
test with the variance correction of Hamed and Rao (1998). Townships whose corrected variance is
negative are listed as "not computed".
:::
:::

::: callout-note
## Lag-1 autocorrelation: correlation between consecutive quarters

Serial dependence "is generally quantified by the correlation coefficient between a data point and
its adjacent point", the lag-one serial correlation (Helsel et al., 2020, pp. 246–247). For the
Gi\* series of one township, $x_1, \dots, x_{19}$:

$$r_1 = \frac{\sum_{t=2}^{19} (x_t - \bar{x})(x_{t-1} - \bar{x})}
{\sum_{t=1}^{19} (x_t - \bar{x})^2}$$

$$r_1 = \frac{\sum (\text{quarter} - \text{mean}) \times (\text{previous quarter} - \text{mean})}
{\sum (\text{quarter} - \text{mean})^2}$$

where $\bar{x}$ is the mean of the 19 values. A value near 0 means that the Gi\* of one quarter is
unrelated to the Gi\* of the next quarter. A value near 1 means that high quarters follow high
quarters and low quarters follow low quarters. For 19 independent values, $r_1$ lies within
$\pm 1.96/\sqrt{19} = \pm 0.45$ in about 95% of series, the bound drawn on an `acf()` plot in R. A
value above 0.45 is therefore significant at the 5% level.

Example: six quarters with the values 1, 2, 4, 5, 4 and 2 have a mean of 3. Each quarter's deviation
from the mean is multiplied by the deviation of the quarter before it:

| Quarter | $x_t - \bar{x}$ | $x_{t-1} - \bar{x}$ | Product |
|---------|-----------------|---------------------|---------|
| 2 | −1 | −2 | 2 |
| 3 | 1 | −1 | −1 |
| 4 | 2 | 1 | 2 |
| 5 | 1 | 2 | 2 |
| 6 | −1 | 1 | −1 |

The products sum to 4 and the squared deviations to $4 + 1 + 1 + 4 + 1 + 1 = 12$, so
$r_1 = 4/12 = 0.33$. Most products are positive because low quarters follow low quarters and high
quarters follow high quarters.

Minbya (MMR012005) has the median $r_1$ of the 330 townships, 0.65. Its Gi\* is below −1 in every
quarter from 2021 Q2 to 2022 Q2 and above 3 in 2024 Q1 and Q2. The Mann-Kendall variance of Hamed
and Rao (1998) is larger for a series with positive autocorrelation.
:::

The lag-1 autocorrelation of the Gi\* series has a median of `r round(median(serial$r1), 2)`. The
lag-1 autocorrelation is above `r round(r1_crit, 2)`, the 5% critical value for 19 quarters,
in `r sum(serial$r1 > r1_crit)` of the 330 townships (`r round(100 * mean(serial$r1 > r1_crit))`%).
Some of this correlation arises from the time lag in Gi\*: with `k = 1`, the Gi\* of a quarter
includes the neighbours' values from the previous quarter (@sec-ehsa-classes).

```{r}
#| label: serial-classes
#| echo: false
hr_kept <- \(cl) sum(serial$class == cl & serial$p_hr < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
hr_n <- \(cl) sum(serial$class == cl)
lost_sh <- sum(lost$class == "sporadic hotspot")
lost_sc <- sum(lost$class == "sporadic coldspot")
cons_kept <- hr_kept("consecutive hotspot"); cons_n <- hr_n("consecutive hotspot")
osc_txt <- all_of(hr_kept("oscilating hotspot"), hr_n("oscilating hotspot"))
osc_n <- hr_n("oscilating hotspot")
mdy_n <- n_in("consecutive hotspot", "Mandalay") + n_in("oscilating hotspot", "Mandalay")
```

The classes in @sec-ehsa-classes use the uncorrected test (@sec-bin). The corrected test was
applied to the `r sig_n` townships with a Mann-Kendall p-value below 0.05:

- **Still significant:** `r kept_n` townships have a corrected p-value below 0.05.
- **No longer significant:** `r nrow(lost)` townships have a corrected p-value of 0.05 or above,
  including `r lost_sh` sporadic hot spots and `r lost_sc` sporadic cold spots.
- **No corrected result:** for `r na_ts`, the corrected variance is negative, so the corrected test
  statistic is undefined.

The consecutive and oscillating hot spots are the hot spots with hot quarters at the end of the
study period (@sec-ehsa-classes). Mandalay Region has `r mdy_n` of these `r cons_n + osc_n`
townships. After the correction, `r cons_kept` of the `r cons_n` consecutive hot spots remain
significant. Of the oscillating hot spots, `r osc_txt` remain significant.

## Sensitivity to the time bin {#sec-ehsa-sensitivity}

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Output

```{r}
#| label: ehsa-monthly
#| echo: false
months <- seq(as.Date("2021-01-01"), as.Date("2025-09-01"), by = "month")
cube_m <- pts |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  count(TS_PCODE, month = floor_date(event_date, "month"), name = "armed") |>
  complete(TS_PCODE = tsp$TS_PCODE, month = months, fill = list(armed = 0)) |>
  mutate(t = as.integer(factor(month))) |>
  arrange(TS_PCODE, t) |>
  spacetime(geo, .loc_col = "TS_PCODE", .time_col = "t") |>
  activate("geometry") |>
  mutate(nb = nb_self, wt = wt_self) |>
  set_nbs("nb") |> set_wts("wt") |>
  activate("data")

set.seed(2610)
ehsa_m <- emerging_hotspot_analysis(cube_m, .var = "armed", k = 1, nsim = 99,
                                    nb_col = "nb", wt_col = "wt") |>
  mutate(class_m = if_else(p_value < 0.05, classification, "not significant"))

bins <- tibble(quarterly = ehsa$class, monthly = ehsa_m$class_m)
hot_cold_switch <- sum(grepl("hotspot", bins$quarterly) & grepl("coldspot", bins$monthly)) +
  sum(grepl("coldspot", bins$quarterly) & grepl("hotspot", bins$monthly))
mean(bins$quarterly == bins$monthly)
count(bins, quarterly, monthly) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = monthly, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  kable()
bin_diff <- bins$quarterly != bins$monthly
n_diff <- sum(bin_diff)
n_ns <- sum(bin_diff & (bins$quarterly == "not significant" | bins$monthly == "not significant"))
n_sp_np <- sum(bin_diff & ((grepl("sporadic", bins$quarterly) & grepl("no pattern", bins$monthly)) |
                             (grepl("no pattern", bins$quarterly) & grepl("sporadic", bins$monthly))))
switch_text <- if (hot_cold_switch == 1) "township changes" else "townships change"
```

The quarterly and monthly cubes give the same class
to `r round(100 * mean(bins$quarterly == bins$monthly))`% of the townships. Of the `r n_diff`
townships with a different class, `r n_ns` involve "not significant" and `r n_sp_np` are between a
sporadic class and no pattern detected. Boschan and Roman (2024) suggest that six-month bins might
reveal diminishing hot spots that are absent from their annual classes. The monthly cube
has `r sum(grepl("diminishing|intensifying", bins$monthly))` diminishing or intensifying townships.
From the quarterly to the monthly cube, `r hot_cold_switch` `r switch_text` between a hot spot
class and a cold spot class.

# Value-added analysis {#sec-value-added}

The value-added analyses stay within local measures of spatial association. Local Moran's I is
compared before and after the start of Operation 1027 on 27 October 2023, to test whether the
clusters moved (RQ4). Bivariate local Moran's I tests whether violence against civilians is
concentrated where battles are concentrated. A univariate map shows where each event type clusters
on its own. The bivariate statistic links the violence against civilians in a township to the
battles in its neighbours, so it can show a township with many events of violence against
civilians next to townships with few battles (RQ3).

## Clusters before and after Operation 1027 {#sec-phases}

Global Moran's I fell from `r round(max(moran_q$I), 2)` in `r peak_label`
to `r round(moran_q$I[19], 2)` in the third quarter of 2025 (@sec-moran-quarter). The quarterly Gi\*
maps show hot spots in northern Shan and Rakhine from the fourth quarter of 2023 (@sec-gi-quarter).
A comparison of the local clusters before and after 27 October 2023 shows which townships were in a
cluster before that date and which were in one afterwards. Mack and Kam (2018) map LISA clusters in
three phases to study change in Africa. Boschan and Roman (2024) compare hot spot maps before and
after an intervention. Here the period is divided at 27 October 2023, the start of Operation 1027.
Local Moran's I is computed in each phase on events per month, so that the phases, which differ in
length, can be compared.

Insurgents attacked military outposts in northern Shan, Kayah and Rakhine from late October 2023,
and the military began forced conscription in February 2024, four months later (Council on Foreign
Relations, 2026). The comparison of the periods before and after 27 October 2023 combines the
effects of the offensive and of conscription.

The coup (1 February 2021), the start of Operation 1027 (27 October 2023) and the start of
conscription (February 2024) are marked on the monthly chart of armed events in @sec-bin.

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Table

```{r}
#| label: phases
#| echo: false
cut_date <- as.Date("2023-10-27")
months_in <- c(before = as.numeric(cut_date - as.Date("2021-01-01")) / 30.4375,
               after = as.numeric(as.Date("2025-10-01") - cut_date) / 30.4375)

phase_rates <- pts |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(phase = if_else(event_date < cut_date, "before", "after")) |>
  count(TS_PCODE, phase) |>
  complete(TS_PCODE = tsp$TS_PCODE, phase = c("before", "after"), fill = list(n = 0)) |>
  mutate(per_month = n / months_in[phase]) |>
  select(-n) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = phase, values_from = per_month)

tsp_ph <- tsp |> select(TS_PCODE, TS, ST) |> left_join(phase_rates, by = "TS_PCODE")

set.seed(2610)
phase_lisa <- map(c(before = "before", after = "after"), \(v) {
  lm <- local_moran(tsp_ph[[v]], nb, wt, nsim = 999)
  factor(if_else(lm$p_ii_sim < 0.05, as.character(lm$median), "Not significant"),
         levels = names(lisa_colours))
})
tsp_ph <- tsp_ph |> mutate(cl_before = phase_lisa$before, cl_after = phase_lisa$after)

set.seed(2610)
ph_tab <- tibble(phase = c("before, 1 Jan 2021 to 26 Oct 2023", "after, 27 Oct 2023 to 30 Sep 2025"),
       months = round(months_in, 1),
       `events per month` = c(sum(tsp_ph$before), sum(tsp_ph$after)),
       `Moran's I` = c(global_moran_perm(tsp_ph$before, nb, wt, nsim = 999)$statistic,
                       global_moran_perm(tsp_ph$after, nb, wt, nsim = 999)$statistic))
kable(ph_tab, digits = c(0, 1, 0, 3), format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
ph_epm <- format(round(ph_tab[["events per month"]]), big.mark = ",")
ph_I <- round(ph_tab[["Moran's I"]], 2)
```

::: callout-note
## Cohen's kappa: agreement beyond chance

The share of townships in the same class before and after 27 October 2023 is inflated by the
townships that are not significant in either phase, which are in the same class by chance. Of the
330 townships, `r sum(tsp_ph$cl_before == "Not significant" & tsp_ph$cl_after == "Not significant")`
are not significant in either phase. Cohen's kappa (Cohen, 1960) removes the agreement expected by
chance:

$$\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e}$$

$$\kappa = \frac{\text{observed agreement} - \text{agreement expected by chance}}
{1 - \text{agreement expected by chance}}$$

where $p_o$ is the share of townships in the same class in both phases, and $p_e$ is the share
expected if the classes of the two phases were independent: for each class, the share of townships
in that class before 27 October 2023 multiplied by the share after it, summed over the classes. A
kappa of 1 means identical classes, and a kappa of 0 means agreement equal to chance. A kappa of
0.45, for example, means that the observed agreement covers 45% of the gap between chance agreement
and identical classes. Boschan and Roman (2024, Table 3) compare hot spot maps of two periods with a
spatial fuzzy version of the statistic, which "captures the strength of the statistical relationship
that underlies the comparison, somewhat like the use of a correlation coefficient" (p. 6).
:::

```{r}
#| label: phase-lists
#| echo: false
moved <- \(from, to) tsp_ph |> st_drop_geometry() |> filter(cl_before == from, cl_after == to) |>
  mutate(x = paste0(TS, " (", ST, ")")) |> pull(x)
joined_hh <- moved("Not significant", "High-High")
left_hh <- moved("High-High", "Not significant")
stayed_hh <- moved("High-High", "High-High")
ph_st <- \(from, to) st_drop_geometry(tsp_ph)$ST[tsp_ph$cl_before == from & tsp_ph$cl_after == to]
stay_tab <- sort(table(ph_st("High-High", "High-High")), decreasing = TRUE)
stay_txt <- knitr::combine_words(paste(stay_tab, "in", names(stay_tab)), oxford_comma = FALSE)
left_sag <- sum(ph_st("High-High", "Not significant") == "Sagaing")
ll_join_st <- st_drop_geometry(tsp_ph)$ST[tsp_ph$cl_before != "Low-Low" & tsp_ph$cl_after == "Low-Low"]
ll_left_st <- st_drop_geometry(tsp_ph)$ST[tsp_ph$cl_before == "Low-Low" & tsp_ph$cl_after != "Low-Low"]
ygn_ll_after <- sum(tsp_ph$ST == "Yangon" & tsp_ph$cl_after == "Low-Low")
```

The number of armed events per month rose from `r ph_epm[1]` before 27 October 2023 to `r ph_epm[2]`
after it. Global Moran's I fell from `r ph_I[1]` before 27 October 2023 to `r ph_I[2]` after it, so
townships with high counts were less often next to each other in the later period. The Low-Low
classes also changed:

- **Low-Low only from 27 October 2023 (`r length(ll_join_st)`):** `r sum(ll_join_st == "Yangon")`
  are in Yangon Region. After that date, `r ygn_ll_after` of the `r sum(tsp$ST == "Yangon")`
  townships of Yangon Region are Low-Low.
- **Low-Low only before 27 October 2023
  (`r length(ll_left_st)`):** `r sum(ll_left_st == "Ayeyarwady")` are in the Ayeyarwady delta
  and `r sum(ll_left_st == "Rakhine")` on the southern Rakhine coast.

Each band in the diagram below joins a local Moran class before 27 October 2023 to a class from that
date, with a width equal to the number of townships and a colour that matches the significant class
of the pair.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.3
cls <- names(lisa_colours)
gap <- 20
tr <- transitions |>
  mutate(from = factor(cl_before, cls), to = factor(cl_after, cls)) |>
  arrange(from, to) |>
  mutate(y0_from = cumsum(n) - n + (as.integer(from) - 1) * gap) |>
  arrange(to, from) |>
  mutate(y0_to = cumsum(n) - n + (as.integer(to) - 1) * gap, id = row_number(),
         end = if_else(from == "Not significant", to, from))
side <- function(col, x) tr |>
  group_by(cl = .data[[col]]) |>
  summarise(n = sum(n), y0 = min(.data[[paste0("y0_", col)]])) |>
  mutate(x = x)
blocks <- bind_rows(side("from", 0), side("to", 1))
s <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 40)
w <- 3 * s^2 - 2 * s^3
ribbons <- tr |>
  reframe(x = c(0.06 + 0.88 * s, rev(0.06 + 0.88 * s)),
          y = c(y0_from + (y0_to - y0_from) * w, rev(y0_from + n + (y0_to - y0_from) * w)),
          .by = c(id, end))
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = ribbons, aes(x, -y, group = id, fill = end), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_rect(data = blocks, aes(xmin = x - 0.06 * (x == 1),
                               xmax = x + 0.06 * (x == 0), ymin = -y0, ymax = -(y0 + n),
                               fill = cl), colour = "white") +
  geom_text(data = blocks, aes(x = if_else(x == 0, -0.02, 1.02), y = -(y0 + n / 2),
                               label = paste0(cl, " (", n, ")"), hjust = if_else(x == 0, 1, 0)),
            size = 3.2) +
  geom_text(data = filter(tr, n >= 4),
            aes(x = 0.1, y = -(y0_from + n / 2) - (y0_to - y0_from) * (3 * 0.05^2 - 2 * 0.05^3),
                label = n), size = 2.9, colour = "grey15") +
  annotate("text", x = c(0, 1), y = 22, hjust = c(1, 0), fontface = "bold", size = 3.4,
           label = c("Before 27 October 2023", "From 27 October 2023")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = lisa_colours, guide = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-0.75, 1.75), ylim = c(-max(blocks$y0 + blocks$n) - 2, 30)) +
  theme_void()
```

- **High-High before and from 27 October 2023 (`r length(stayed_hh)`):** `r stay_txt`.
- **High-High only before 27 October 2023 (`r length(left_hh)`):** `r left_sag` of them are in

- **Context:** Su Mon (2024) describes resistance groups blocking military reinforcements on the

  December 2024.

Cohen's kappa for the classes before and after 27 October 2023
is `r round((po - pe) / (1 - pe), 2)`, on a scale from 0 (agreement equal to chance) to 1 (identical
classes). The raw agreement of `r round(100 * po)`% is partly chance: `r round(100 * pe)`% of the
townships would be in the same class if the classes of the two phases were independent. The kappa
lies between the two values of Boschan and Roman (2024, Table 3), 0.583 for all features and 0.333
for significant features only.

## Violence against civilians near battles {#sec-bivariate}

Slide 28 of the Lesson 5 deck gives the formula of global bivariate Moran's I, and slide 29 the
meaning of its four classes. Fergen and Bergstrom (2021) use bivariate LISA to ask whether one
variable in a county is associated with another variable in the neighbouring counties. Here
bivariate local Moran's I tests whether violence against civilians in a township is associated with
battles in the neighbouring townships.

::: callout-note
## Bivariate local Moran's I

The bivariate statistic is the product of the township's standardised count of violence against
civilians and the average standardised count of battles in its neighbours:

$$I_i^B = z_{v,i} \sum_j w_{ij} \, z_{b,j}$$

$$\text{bivariate } I = \text{violence } z \times \text{neighbours' average battle } z$$

where $z_{v,i}$ is the standardised count of violence against civilians in township $i$, $z_{b,j}$
is the standardised count of battles in township $j$, and $w_{ij}$ is the row-standardised weight.
Up to a constant, $I_i^B$ is the term of township $i$ in the sum on slide 28. A township is
High-High when its count of violence against civilians and its neighbours' average battle count are
both above their medians, and High-Low when the first is above its median and the second below.
Significance is tested by permutation with 999 draws, as for local Moran's I.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}
#### Table

```{r}
#| label: bivariate
#| echo: false
set.seed(2610)
bv <- local_moran_bv(tsp$vac, tsp$battles, nb, wt, nsim = 999)
z_vac <- as.numeric(scale(tsp$vac))
lag_battles <- st_lag(as.numeric(scale(tsp$battles)), nb, wt)
hi_vac <- z_vac > median(z_vac)
hi_bat <- lag_battles > median(lag_battles)

tsp_bv <- tsp |>
  select(TS, ST, vac, battles) |>
  mutate(Ib = bv$Ib, p = pmin(1, 2 * bv$p_sim),
         cluster = case_when(p >= 0.05 ~ "Not significant",
                             hi_vac & hi_bat ~ "High-High",
                             !hi_vac & !hi_bat ~ "Low-Low",
                             hi_vac ~ "High-Low",
                             .default = "Low-High"),
         cluster = factor(cluster, names(lisa_colours)))
count(st_drop_geometry(tsp_bv), cluster) |> kable()
bv_n <- \(cl, st) sum(tsp_bv$cluster == cl & tsp_bv$ST %in% st)
bv_hh_c <- bv_n("High-High", c("Sagaing", "Magway", "Mandalay"))
hl_other <- st_drop_geometry(tsp_bv) |> filter(cluster == "High-Low", ST != "Yangon")
lh <- st_drop_geometry(tsp_bv) |> filter(cluster == "Low-High")
ygn_vac_hh <- sum(tl$type == "Violence against civilians" & tl$cluster == "High-High" & tl$ST == "Yangon")
ygn_vac_txt <- if (ygn_vac_hh == 0) "no High-High townships" else paste(ygn_vac_hh, "High-High townships")
lh_txt <- knitr::combine_words(paste0(lh$TS, " (", lh$ST, ")"), oxford_comma = FALSE)
hl_other_txt <- paste0(knitr::combine_words(hl_other$TS, oxford_comma = FALSE), ", in ",
                       knitr::combine_words(unique(hl_other$ST), oxford_comma = FALSE))
```

```{r}
#| ref.label: "bivariate"
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="false" title="How the code works"}
`local_moran_bv()` returns `Ib` and a one-sided pseudo p-value, which `pmin(1, 2 * bv$p_sim)`
doubles to match the two-sided tests elsewhere. The class compares the township's standardised count
of violence against civilians and its neighbours' average standardised battle count (`st_lag()`)
with their medians (@sec-lisa-labels).

The mean of `vac` over all townships is 30.12 and its standard deviation is 35.72, so `z_vac` for
Myawaddy is $(36 - 30.12) / 35.72 = 0.165$. `Ib` is the product of `z_vac` and `lag_battles`. For
Myawaddy, $0.165 \times 1.694 = 0.279$. The median of `z_vac` is −0.339 and the median of
`lag_battles` is −0.214, so Bago (−0.115 and −0.574) is High-Low: its count of violence against
civilians is below the mean and above the median. Mohnyin has `p_sim` of 0.029, and the doubled value of 0.058
is above 0.05, so Mohnyin is "Not significant".

```{r}
                   fun.geometry = st_point_on_surface, size = 2.8, label.size = 0.15,
                   min.segment.length = 0, box.padding = 0.5, force = 3, max.overlaps = Inf,
                   seed = 1) +
  gg_key(c10_win[["xmin"]] + 2000, c10_win[["ymin"]] + 2500,
         c10_win[["ymax"]] - c10_win[["ymin"]], km = 10) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c10_cols, guide = "none") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c10_win[c(1, 3)], ylim = c10_win[c(2, 4)], datum = NA, expand = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "Yangon: the box on the left map") +
  theme_void(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
        panel.border = element_rect(fill = NA, colour = "grey60"))
c10_main + c10_zoom + plot_layout(widths = c(1.5, 1)) +
  plot_annotation(title = "High-Low and Low-High townships of the bivariate statistic",
                  theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13)))
```

#### Code

```{r}
#| ref.label: "bivariate-named"
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
```
:::

- **High-High (`r sum(tsp_bv$cluster == "High-High")`):** `r bv_hh_c` are in the central dry
  zone, `r bv_n("High-High", "Tanintharyi")` in Tanintharyi, `r bv_n("High-High", "Kayin")` in Kayin
  and `r bv_n("High-High", "Shan (North)")` in northern Shan.
- **High-Low (`r sum(tsp_bv$cluster == "High-Low")`):** these townships have violence against
  civilians above the median next to battle counts below the
  median. `r sum(tsp_bv$cluster == "High-Low" & tsp_bv$ST == "Yangon")` of them are in Yangon
  Region. The others are `r hl_other_txt`. Su Mon (2024) describes resistance groups assassinating
  military-appointed administrators. The same source describes civilians detained by the military or
  by resistance groups as suspected informants. The pattern in Yangon is consistent with targeted
  violence of this kind.
- **Low-High (`r nrow(lh)`):** `r lh_txt`. Violence against civilians is below the median, next to
  battle counts above the median. Civilians in these townships may be targeted less often, may have
  left, or may be reported less often.

The univariate map of violence against civilians (@sec-lmsa-types) has `r ygn_vac_txt` in Yangon, so
the Yangon pattern is visible only in the bivariate map.

# Integrated findings and discussion {#sec-discussion}

## Answers to the research questions

| Question | Answer | Evidence |
|----------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------|
| RQ1. Clusters and outliers | `r nrow(hh)` High-High townships with `r round(100 * hh_share)`% of all armed events, `r central$n` of them in the central dry zone | @sec-lmsa |
| RQ2. Emergence and change | `r n_in("consecutive hotspot", "Mandalay") + n_in("oscilating hotspot", "Mandalay")` of the `r n_class("consecutive hotspot") + n_class("oscilating hotspot")` consecutive and oscillating hot spots are in Mandalay Region | @sec-ehsa |
| RQ3. Three kinds of violence | The central dry zone is High-High for all three kinds of violence; `r sum(tsp_bv$cluster == "High-Low" & tsp_bv$ST == "Yangon")` Yangon townships have violence against civilians next to few battles (bivariate High-Low) | @sec-lmsa-types, @sec-bivariate |
| RQ4. After October 2023 | Events per month rose from `r ph_epm[1]` to `r ph_epm[2]`, and global Moran's I fell from `r ph_I[1]` to `r ph_I[2]` | @sec-phases |

```{r}
#| label: rq-detail
#| echo: false
se_sizes <- sort(hh_blocks$n[hh_blocks$n > 1 & hh_blocks$n < central$n])
rm_sag <- sum(tsp$ST[match(rm_hh, tsp$TS_PCODE)] == "Sagaing")
border_b <- range(mix$battles[mix$area %in% border])
ygn_cc <- all_of(sum(ehsa$class == "consecutive coldspot" & ehsa$ST == "Yangon"),
                 n_class("consecutive coldspot"))
hh_one <- filter(hh_blocks, n == 1)
hh_one_txt <- paste0(cw(paste0(hh_one$towns, " in ", hh_one$states)),
                     if (nrow(hh_one) == 1) " has" else " have")
```

- **RQ1, clusters and outliers:** outside the central dry zone, the High-High townships are in two
  groups on the south-east border, of `r se_sizes[1]` and `r se_sizes[2]` townships. `r hh_one_txt`
  no High-High neighbour. The `r nrow(ll)` Low-Low townships are in Shan, the Ayeyarwady delta,
  Yangon and Nay Pyi Taw. The two outliers are `r cw(outl$TS)` (@sec-local-moran).
- **RQ2, emergence and change:** the Mann-Kendall filter removes `r length(rm_hh)` of
  the `r nrow(hh)` High-High townships of local Moran's I, `r rm_sag` of them in Sagaing.
  In `r all_of(sum(rise_fall$rf), length(rm_hh))` of them, Gi\* rose and then
  fell (@sec-ehsa-filter). Of the consecutive cold spots, `r ygn_cc` are in Yangon
  Region (@sec-ehsa-classes).
- **RQ3, three kinds of violence:** battles are `r round(border_b[1])`% to `r round(border_b[2])`%
  of the events in the north, the south-east border and the west (@sec-areas). Violence against
  civilians is `r round(pct("Central dry zone", "vac"))`% of the events in the central dry zone. In
  the bivariate map, `r sum(tsp_bv$cluster == "High-Low" & tsp_bv$ST == "Yangon")` Yangon townships
  are High-Low (@sec-bivariate).
- **RQ4, after October 2023:** `r length(joined_hh)` townships are High-High only after 27
  October 2023. They are north of Mandalay, in northern Shan, in northern Rakhine, on the Thai border in
  Kayin and in Bago (East) (@sec-phases).

## Comparison with the provided papers

| Comparison | Provided paper | This report |
|------------------|--------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| Clustering over time | Mack and Kam (2018): violence against civilians in Africa clustered in every year | Armed events clustered in every quarter (@sec-moran-quarter) |
| Location of hot spots | Mack and Kam (2018): many hot spots near borders between countries | High-High townships on the south-east border, and the largest cluster in the central dry zone |
| Local Moran's I against Gi\* | Khan et al. (2017): local Moran's I confirmed the Gi\* hot and cold spots | Every High-High township is a Gi\* hot spot, and `r sum(lisa$cluster == "Low-Low" & gistar$spot == "Cold spot")` of the `r nrow(ll)` Low-Low townships are Gi\* cold spots |
| Persistence of hot spots | Khan et al. (2017): 91% of the 2003 hot spot counties still hot in 2012 | Of the `r length(stayed_hh) + length(left_hh)` townships that were High-High before 27 October 2023, `r length(stayed_hh)` (`r round(100 * length(stayed_hh) / (length(stayed_hh) + length(left_hh)))`%) were High-High after it |
| EHSA classes | Boschan and Roman (2024): hot spot classes only (new, consecutive, persistent and sporadic) | Cold spot classes hold `r sum(grepl("coldspot", ehsa$class))` townships, hot spot classes `r sum(grepl("hotspot", ehsa$class))`, no pattern detected `r n_class("no pattern detected")`, and `r n_class("not significant")` are not significant |

- **Central dry zone:** the largest cluster is in the central dry zone, where little fighting was
  recorded in the decades before 2021 (Su Mon, 2024). The hot spots of Mack and Kam (2018) are near
  borders between countries.
- **Many cold spots:** the study areas differ. Boschan and Roman (2024) studied shootings in South
  Philadelphia, one part of a city. In Myanmar, `r round(100 * zero_q)`% of township-quarters have
  no armed event.

## Alternative explanations

- **Reporting.** ACLED records events reported by its sources. Fewer events may be recorded than
  occurred in areas closed to observers, so some cold spots may be gaps in reporting. Four of the
  eight townships with no recorded event are in districts governed by the United Wa State
  Army (@sec-prep), where reporting may be limited.
- **Population.** A township with more people may have more armed events. Townships with high rates
  per 100,000 people are also neighbours of each other: Moran's I of the log rate
  is `r round(cr[["Moran's I"]][3], 2)` (@sec-count-rate). Population size may therefore explain
  only part of the clustering of the counts.
- **Location precision.** Geo-precision 2 events are placed at a nearby town. The clusters of
  township counts may depend in part on the locations of those towns. Geo-precision 2 events
  are `r round(100 * mean(pts$geo_precision == 2))`% of the events analysed (@sec-precision), so an
  effect of location precision cannot be excluded.

# Implications for peace-building {#sec-implications}

```{r}
#| label: implications
#| echo: false
n_pi <- sum(grepl("persistent hotspot|intensifying hotspot", ehsa$classification))
n_matman_pc <- sum(ehsa$classification == "persistent coldspot" &
                     tsp$DT[match(ehsa$location, tsp$TS_PCODE)] == "Matman")
n_matman_pc <- c("No", "One", "Two", "Three", "Four", "Five")[n_matman_pc + 1]
```

The maps describe where armed conflict has been recorded. ACLED records reported events, so the
implications below concern where events are recorded, and not their causes or the needs of the
population. The townships named below are labelled on the maps of @sec-bivariate and
@sec-ehsa-classes.

- **Violence against civilians next to battles:** in the High-High townships of the bivariate
  map (@sec-bivariate), in the central dry zone, Tanintharyi, Kayin and northern Shan, violence
  against civilians and battles are both recorded in neighbouring townships. Su Mon (2024) describes
  the military turning "to the closest civilian population center to detain, torture, and kill"
  after losses, and rivalry between resistance groups that "can impede the delivery of humanitarian
  aid". Protection of civilians and humanitarian access may be priorities in these townships.
- **Violence against civilians next to few battles:** in
  the `r sum(tsp_bv$cluster == "High-Low" & tsp_bv$ST == "Yangon")` High-Low townships of Yangon,
  violence against civilians is above the median and the battle counts of the neighbours are below
  it. Su Mon (2024) describes resistance groups that "opportunistically assassinate
  military-appointed administrators" and civilians "detained by the military or resistance groups
  under the impression of being informants". Monitoring of detentions and targeted killings may be
  relevant in these townships.
- **Hot quarters at the end of the period:** Kim and Lee (2023, p. 8) give priority to "persistent
  hotspots or intensifying hotspots" of wildlife-vehicle collisions on expressways. In this
  report, `r if (n_pi == 0) "no township is" else paste(n_pi, "townships are")` in either class. The
  consecutive and oscillating hot spots, around Mandalay and in Nawnghkio in northern
  Shan (@sec-ehsa-classes), are hot in the last quarters of the period, so they may be the first
  places for monitoring.
- **Cold spots:** a cold spot has few recorded events, which may come from little fighting or from
  little reporting. `r n_matman_pc` of the `r all_n("persistent coldspot")` persistent cold spots
  before the filter are in Matman District, which the United Wa State Army has governed since its
  ceasefire of May 1989 (@sec-prep). Verification of reporting in these townships may be needed
  before they are treated as quiet.

# Limitations {#sec-limitations}

| Limitation | Effect on the results |
|--------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------|
| Reported events only | Cold spots and zero counts may partly reflect limited access for reporters |
| Equal weight per event | A skirmish and an airstrike count the same. Fatalities are mapped for description only |
| Population projection for 2023 from the 2014 census | The projection uses internal migration rates from the 2014 census (OCHA, 2023), so displacement since 2021 is not in it. It gives Hlaingtharya (East) `r format(hl$pop[hl$TS == "Hlaingtharya (East)"], big.mark = ",")` people (@sec-count-rate) |
| Counts as the analysis variable | Townships with high rates per 100,000 people are also neighbours of each other: Moran's I of the log rate is `r round(cr[["Moran's I"]][3], 2)` (@sec-count-rate) |
| Location precision | `r round(100 * mean(pts$geo_precision == 2))`% of the events analysed have geo-precision code 2 and are placed at a nearby town (@sec-precision) |
| Township as the unit | Clusters may depend on township boundaries. Results for districts or a grid may differ |
| Contiguity neighbours | k-nearest neighbour weights change the local Moran class of `r changed_pct[1]`% ($k = 6$) and `r changed_pct[2]`% ($k = 8$) of the townships; global Moran's I is significant at p ≤ 0.001 under all three weights (@sec-weights-check) |
| Monotonic trends only | The p < 0.05 filter removes the `r length(rm_hh)` High-High townships in which Gi\* rose and then fell (@sec-ehsa-filter) |
| Multiple comparisons | `r fdr_hh + fdr_ll` of the `r nrow(hh) + nrow(ll)` High-High and Low-Low townships remain significant after the FDR correction (@sec-fdr). The 330 Mann-Kendall tests of the emerging hot spot classes are not corrected |
| Time bin | `r round(100 * mean(bins$quarterly != bins$monthly))`% of the townships change class between the quarterly and monthly cubes, mostly to or from "not significant"; `r hot_cold_switch` `r switch_text` between a hot spot class and a cold spot class (@sec-ehsa-sensitivity) |
| Serial correlation in the Gi\* series | `r nrow(lost)` of `r sig_n` townships with a significant Mann-Kendall trend lose significance after the correction (@sec-serial) |
| Phase comparison | The offensive of October 2023 and conscription from February 2024 fall in the same phase, so the comparison combines their effects (@sec-phases) |
